Required spine: B00 INTRO (cold open, ask answered) -> B01 PROBLEM -> cycle 1 [B02 CLI(ASK) -> B03 CODE -> B04 OUTPUT] -> cycle 2 = required revision [B05 CLI(CHANGE) -> B06 CODE -> B07 OUTPUT] -> B08 SUMMARY -> B09 NEXT STEPS (handoff) -> B10 OUTRO. THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW: code/naive_similarity.py and code/embedding_similarity.py in this reel folder are REAL, runnable Python, actually executed before authoring B04/B07 — their `lines` are verbatim (trimmed) captured stdout, not invented. embedding_similarity.py depends on the free, local `sentence-transformers` package (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a real Sentence-BERT model per Reimers & Gurevych 2019, already cited in this chapter's SOURCES.md via the sibling ai-explainer reel) — no API key, downloaded once from Hugging Face's public model hub. Build note: this package was installed and run inside an ISOLATED venv (not the toolkit's shared system Python), because sentence-transformers pulls a numpy version that conflicts with kokoro-onnx's own numpy pin — installing it system-wide broke `kokoro_onnx` import until reverted. Anyone re-running code/embedding_similarity.py should use its own venv (`python -m venv <env>` + `pip install sentence-transformers`), never the toolkit's own Python. Honesty note: the chapter's own Figure 02 is captioned as 'a 2-dimensional embedding-space sketch' (a teaching simplification, like Fig 01) — it is not a literal claim that any specific embedding model separates the exact four short quoted phrases by a wide margin. Tested directly: several general-purpose Sentence-BERT models (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2, all-mpnet-base-v2, paraphrase-mpnet-base-v2) do NOT cleanly reproduce that exact separation on those four bare 5-7 word fragments in isolation — short, decontextualized questions are genuinely hard even for real embeddings. What DOES reproduce cleanly and honestly, and is what this reel actually shows, is the retrieval framing the chapter itself is building toward: given a realistic small set of FAQ passages and one real question, word-overlap retrieval gets fooled by a literally shared phrase ('how do i request') and returns the wrong passage, while all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings correctly rank the semantically right passage first. Verified directly — see code/ and the captured stdout in B04/B07.

props.title: naive_similarity.py — Claude Code output
props.code:
# naive_similarity.py — retrieve an FAQ passage by literal word overlap
PASSAGES = {
    "HR-01": "Vacation and PTO: full-time employees accrue 15 paid days "
             "off per year, usable for vacation, personal time, or "
             "appointments.",
    "IT-01": "How do I request a new laptop? Submit a hardware ticket "
             "through the IT service desk portal.",
    # ...4 more passages (HR-02/03, IT-02/03)
}
QUERY = "How do I request time off?"

def word_overlap(a, b):
    wa, wb = tokenize(a), tokenize(b)
    return len(wa & wb) / len(wa | wb)   # shared words ÷ all words

props.title: embedding_similarity.py — Claude Code output
props.code:
# embedding_similarity.py — same query, same 6 passages, real Sentence-BERT
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")  # free, local, no API key

passage_embeddings = model.encode(texts)
query_embedding = model.encode(QUERY)

def cosine(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

# rank PASSAGES by cosine(query_embedding, passage_embedding)
